title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Theorem §44 of E449. Let P be prime and Q = P−1. Assuming a primitive root a exists (a has multiplicative order exactly Q mod P), every power a^n with gcd(n,Q)=1 is again a primitive root. Hence there are as many primitive roots in 1..P−1 as there are integers below Q that are coprime to Q, namely φ(P−1).

Proof on this page:
(i) Because a is primitive, a^e ≡ 1 (mod P) exactly when Q | e. So a^{Qn} ≡ 1.
(ii) Suppose a^{mn} ≡ 1 with 0 < m < Q. Then mn = kQ for some k. Euler writes this as m:Q = k:n and concludes that n and Q would not be coprime. In modern terms, gcd(n,Q)=1 forces Q | m, which is impossible for 0 < m < Q.
(iii) Therefore the period of the residues of 1, a^n, a^{2n}, … is exactly Q. The 'series of residues' is complete, so the residue b of a^n is a primitive root.
(iv) Each n < Q coprime to Q gives a primitive root. So there are φ(Q) of them. The converse (no others) is deferred to Scholion §48.

Corollary §45 starts the numerical check:
- P=3: the single primitive root is 2.
- P=5: the primitive roots are 2 and 3.
- The next page continues with P=7 and P=11.
- The next page also gives the product formula for φ(Q).

In modern terms: ord(a^n) = Q/gcd(n,Q), and the number of generators of the cyclic group (Z/P)^* is φ(P−1).
errors: The existence of a primitive root is simply assumed here ('cum certe detur radix primitiua'). It rests on Euler's earlier argument in this paper, which Gauss (Disquisitiones, art. 56) judged insufficient.
The previous page's claim that b 'vtique ab a erit diuersum' fails for n=1, where b=a. This is a trivial slip.
The step from m:Q = k:n to 'n and Q not coprime' is stated loosely (as a proportion) but is valid. Coprimality forces Q | m, contradicting m < Q.

Only sufficiency (n coprime to Q ⇒ a^n primitive) is proved on this page. The count 'tot dari' as an equality needs the converse and the distinctness of the a^n mod P. These are addressed in Scholion §48; distinctness follows from the period being Q.

ideas.what: If a is a primitive root mod a prime P and gcd(n,P−1)=1, then a^n is also a primitive root (order of a power in a cyclic group).
ideas.modern_name: ord(g^n) = ord(g)/gcd(n, ord(g)); generators of a cyclic group
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E449, 1774), systematized by Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), arts. 53–56

ideas.what: The number of primitive roots mod prime P equals the number of integers below P−1 that are coprime to P−1.
ideas.modern_name: There are φ(p−1) primitive roots mod p
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E449); Gauss DA art. 53 ff. acknowledges Euler

ideas.what: The lemma that mn = kQ with gcd(n,Q)=1 and m < Q is impossible.
ideas.modern_name: Euclid's lemma / Gauss's lemma on divisibility
ideas.where_published: standard; used throughout Euler's number theory

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known and correctly credited E449 result that there are φ(p−1) primitive roots, with a standard and correct proof conditional on the existence of a primitive root. Nothing here is absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image closely. The image reads 'existente m <̄ Q', a typographic mark for '<'. No substantive corrections are needed.
